summary: Defines relationships for composing a complete path metric from metrics of its sub-paths, so end-to-end network performance can be estimated from measurements of the parts. This is called spatial composition in RFC 2330.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6049 explains how to estimate a network path's delay, loss and delay variation from measurements of its smaller parts. The result is an estimate, not a direct measurement, and works only when the parts and measurements meet stated conditions.

questions: what is spatial composition of metrics
how to compose packet loss from sub-paths
how to estimate end to end delay from sub-path measurements
subtitle: How separately measured network segments can estimate delay, packet loss and delay variation end to end.

tldr.problem: A complete source-to-destination path may cross independent networks that cannot share one measurement method or timing schedule.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6049 defines functions that combine measurements from sub-paths, including sums for mean and minimum delay, a probability formula for loss, and two ways to estimate delay variation.
tldr.outcome: A composed value estimates the complete-path metric and depends on assumptions about coverage, timing and independence. RFC 6049 was updated by RFC 6248.

today: RFC 6049 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2011. It has been updated by RFC 6248.

sections.title: Why Compose Path Measurements
sections.content:
Some networks cannot measure directly between the source and destination of interest. A path may cross independent administrative domains with different policies, tools and measurement schedules. RFC 6049 calls the alternative spatial composition: measure separate parts of the path and combine their results.

The RFC defines deterministic functions for estimating complete-path metrics from sub-path metrics. It also warns that these relationships are conjectures with specific assumptions. A sum of individual packet delays, for example, should not be treated as an accurate estimate of one packet's complete-path delay.
sections.plainLanguage: When one measurement cannot cover the whole route, each network can measure its own segment. Combining those results gives an estimate, not a direct measurement of the complete route.

sections.title: Scope and Missing Results
sections.content:
The RFC composes one-way delay, one-way packet loss and packet delay variation. Measurements may use the same or similar test packets, different measurement methods, or active and passive techniques. Inferring a missing segment's value from the complete path and the other segments is outside the scope.

If a measurement cannot start on a sub-path, the result should be marked undefined. This differs from sending packets throughout the interval and finding that all were lost. If any input needed for a composed metric is undefined, the composed result should also be undefined.
sections.plainLanguage: If a network cannot measure one segment, the complete result should be marked unknown. That is different from a test where every sent packet was lost.

sections.title: Conditions and Sources of Error
sections.content:
Composition assumes that sub-path measurements describe the corresponding parts of the complete path. The methodology should use similar packets and synchronized measurement intervals; largely overlapping intervals may be enough. The RFC recommends Poisson or Periodic test streams and requires an assumption that the sub-path measurements are independent for the metric being composed.

Results can differ from the complete path if test packets take different routes, measurement links add extra delay, some network elements are missing, or routing changes. Encapsulation, encryption and fragmentation can also make test packets behave differently. A finite estimate can even result when no complete-path route exists.
sections.plainLanguage: The estimate is more useful when every segment covers the real route and measurements happen at similar times. Different routes, missing links or correlated conditions can make the result wrong.

sections.title: Composing Delay and Packet Loss
sections.content:
For packets that arrive within the allowed waiting time, finite one-way delay is the destination timestamp minus the source timestamp. The RFC estimates the complete-path mean delay by adding the mean finite delays from each sub-path. It estimates the minimum delay by adding the minimum finite delays. These methods require sufficiently large samples and suitable, sufficiently independent delay distributions.

For packet loss, each sub-path has an empirical loss probability, Ep. The complete-path estimate is one minus the product of each sub-path's probability of delivery, expressed as 1 - ((1 - Ep1) × (1 - Ep2) × ... × (1 - EpS)). Correlated loss causes, such as a shared physical failure, can invalidate this assumption.
sections.plainLanguage: For delay, add the measured mean or minimum from each segment. For loss, combine the chance of delivery on every segment to estimate the chance of losing a packet somewhere.

sections.title: Composing Delay Variation
sections.content:
The RFC defines packet delay variation relative to the sample's minimum finite delay. It provides statistics such as the mean, variance, skewness and quantile. Because variation cannot simply be added across segments, the RFC gives two ways to estimate a complete-path quantile.

Approximate convolution combines sub-path delay distributions represented as histograms with 1-ms bins. The Normal Power Approximation combines summary statistics using the referenced ITU-T method. Both depend on stationary, sufficiently independent sub-path distributions; correlation and extreme outliers can increase error.
sections.plainLanguage: Delay variation is not found by adding each segment's variation. The RFC combines distributions or their summary statistics, but correlated delays can make either estimate unreliable.

sections.title: Security and Metric Registration
sections.content:
Measurement traffic could be used for denial-of-service attacks against a destination or an intervening network. The RFC recommends agreements about the timing, size and frequency of tests. Passive measurements must focus on the headers of interest and protect any stored payload; a hash can often be used for payload comparison.

An observer may identify test packets and handle them differently, or inject packets that appear to belong to the sample. Cryptographic packet checks may help detect interference. IANA registered the metrics in the IPPM metrics registry under identities 71 through 83.
sections.plainLanguage: Test traffic can burden networks or be treated differently from ordinary traffic. Operators can agree on limits and use checks to identify interference with measurements.

items.title: Mean delay
items.text: Add the mean finite delay of each sub-path.

items.title: Minimum delay
items.text: Add the minimum finite delay of each sub-path.

items.title: Packet loss
items.text: One minus the product of delivery probabilities across sub-paths.

items.title: Delay variation
items.text: Estimate a quantile by approximate convolution or Normal Power Approximation.
